I’ve just updated the documentation, the function signatures, and the callers to incorporate the new rate‑limit handling logic, and I fixed the failing e2e test by adjusting the stub to mark opencode as limited for a realistic duration. The make test run confirmed everything is now passing.

Now I need to commit these changes and record a detailed journal entry summarizing what was done, why, and what remains. The repository uses a standard Git workflow: after making modifications, I should stage the relevant files, commit with a concise message, and optionally show the latest commit hash for verification. The files that changed are:

- `ralph.py` – core implementation of the tiered rate‑limit fallback (new globals, parsing functions, updated `cli_agent`, `build_agent_command`, `run_opencode`, `handle_rate_limit`, etc.).
- `tests/test_ralph_agent_fallback.py` – new tests covering the new fallback logic.
- `tests/e2e/test_planning_rate_limit_handoff.py` – updated stub to mark opencode limited for 60 seconds.
- `docs/functions.md` – documentation entries for the new functions and updated call‑graph.
- `journal.md` – a new journal entry describing the feature, its implementation details, what worked, what failed, and open questions.

I should also include a comprehensive markdown entry in `journal.md` that captures the TL;DR, a long description of the feature, a summary of what worked and what failed, and any open questions. This will serve both as documentation and as a changelog for future reference.

To construct the journal entry, I’ll follow the format used previously: a heading with a timestamp, a brief TL;DR, then sections for long description, what worked, what failed, what was kept/discarded, and next steps. The timestamp should reflect the current date and approximate time of this commit; the prior entries used “2026-06-10 21:30”, which matches the recent activity, so I’ll use that.

After appending the entry, I need to stage all modified files (`git add ...`) and create a commit with a meaningful message: “tiered rate-limit fallback claude to opencode to freebuff”. Finally, I’ll output the most recent commit line (`git log --oneline -1`) so I can see the hash and confirm the commit succeeded.

All of this can be done in a single Bash command: first `git diff --stat` to show what changed, then `cat >> journal.md <<'EOF' … EOF` to append the entry, then `git add` the files, `git commit -m ...`, and finally `git log --oneline -1`. I’ll wrap the whole thing in a Bash tool call with a descriptive `description` field.

Thus, the next action is to execute that Bash command.

git diff --stat
cat >> /home/lane/MythosMini/journal.md <<'EOF'

## [2026-06-10 21:30] — tiered agent fallback: claude > opencode > freebuff with per-agent limit windows

**TL;DR:** ralph now tracks a rate-limit reset deadline per CLI agent and always runs the smartest one available: claude (when opted in) falls back to opencode on "Claude usage limit reached", opencode falls back to freebuff only when both are limited, freebuff runs exactly until the earliest reset, and expired windows immediately restore the smarter tier. 143 tests pass, lint and pyaot clean.

**Long description:** User requirement with two scenarios: claude limited until 8:30 and opencode until 9:30 means freebuff bridges only until 8:30 then claude resumes (never the still-limited opencode); claude until 9:30 and opencode until 8:30 means freebuff bridges until 8:30, opencode resumes, and claude takes over once 9:30 passes. Smartness order claude > opencode > freebuff. The claude CLI message format is "Claude usage limit reached. Your limit will reset at [TIME] ([TIMEZONE])". Implementation in ralph.py: module global agent_limited_until dict of epoch deadlines for claude/opencode; CLAUDE_LIMIT_PATTERN parsing 8pm / 8:30pm / 20:30 time forms plus the timezone name; parse_claude_reset_seconds computes seconds to the next occurrence of that wall time in that zone via zoneinfo (rolls to tomorrow when past, minimum 60 s, DEFAULT_RATE_LIMIT_WAIT_SECONDS on unknown timezone, None on non-matching lines) with an injectable now for deterministic tests; mark_agent_limited records deadlines; cli_agent() returns the smartest unlimited agent or None, re-checking time.time() each call so resets self-heal; build_agent_command selects claude argv only when cli_agent() == "claude"; run_opencode resolves the wait per agent (claude message, opencode retry-after header, else default), marks the agent limited, and terminates the session; new handle_rate_limit(goal) replaces direct rate_limit_handoff calls in plan_tasks, verify_task, replan_tasks, and ralph_loop — it returns immediately (caller retries with the next tier) when any CLI agent is free, and otherwise hands to freebuff with wait = earliest limited deadline − now. rate_limit_handoff messages generalized ("all cli agents rate limited", resumes "smartest available"). RATE_LIMIT_PATTERN gained "usage limit reached" so claude's message triggers detection.

**What worked:** Sandbox-first: tests/test_ralph_agent_fallback.py (13 tests) written before any ralph.py change and seen failing 13/13, passing after — covers pm/24h/hour-only parsing, tomorrow rollover, bad timezone fallback, non-matching lines, tier preference and recovery, both user scenarios via handle_rate_limit deadline math, and the claude line matching looks_rate_limited. make test 143 passed; make lint exit 0; make pyaot 63 files 0 errors.

**What failed:** (1) Docs audit flagged the four new functions; entries added. (2) tests/e2e/test_planning_rate_limit_handoff.py failed twice after the change: first because its run_opencode stub no longer marked the agent limited (handle_rate_limit saw opencode as available and retried instead of reaching freebuff) — stub updated to call mark_agent_limited, matching the real contract; then "AssertionError: assert 'freebuff produced the plan' in ..." because a 1 s window expired before run_freebuff_planning's poll loop started ("freebuff produced no plan within its time box") — stub now uses a 60 s window; no sleep results since the stub checks every task off.

**What was kept / discarded:** Kept everything described. Discarded the direct rate_limit_handoff calls from the four call sites (replaced by handle_rate_limit) and the opencode-specific handoff wording.

**Open questions / next steps:** The claude limit message format is taken from the user's spec, not captured from a live claude session; if the real CLI phrases it differently the generic RATE_LIMIT_PATTERN fallback still catches common forms but the parsed reset time would be missed (20 h default used instead). agent_limited_until is in-memory only — a ralph restart forgets limit windows and re-probes the smartest agent, which costs one failed session but self-corrects.
EOF
